title: Pole Positions and the Time Signal
intro: Where a pole sits tells you what the signal does: its distance from the origin sets how fast the signal grows or decays, and its angle sets how fast it oscillates.

blocks.text: A single pole at $a$ with a causal ROC is the signal $a^n u[n]$. Moving the pole moves the signal:

items: Inside the unit circle ($|a| < 1$): the samples decay. The closer to the origin, the faster.
On the circle ($|a| = 1$): they neither grow nor decay. $a = 1$ is the unit step.
Outside the circle ($|a| > 1$): they grow without bound.
On the negative real axis ($a < 0$): the samples alternate in sign, $a^n = |a|^n(-1)^n$, the fastest oscillation possible.

blocks.text: Try it with the viewer's decaying exponential: move Radius r from 0.3 to 1.2 and watch the stems in the x[n] panel and the pole cross the dashed unit circle.
A pair of poles, a damped oscillation
A conjugate pair $p = r e^{\pm j\theta}$ gives a damped sinusoid. Each pole contributes $p^n = r^n e^{\pm j\theta n}$, and the two add to a real signal:

blocks.tex: r^n \sin(\theta n)\, u[n] \;\leftrightarrow\; \frac{r\sin\theta\; z}{z^2 - 2r\cos\theta\, z + r^2}, \qquad |z| > r

items: The angle $\theta$ is the oscillation frequency in radians per sample: the signal repeats every $360°/\theta$ samples.
The radius $r$ is the decay per sample: the envelope is $r^n$, which falls to $1/e$ after $1/\ln(1/r)$ samples.
Nearer the unit circle means slower decay, a longer ring, and a sharper peak in the frequency response at $\omega = \theta$. A pole on the circle rings forever.

blocks.text: With $r = 0.9$ and $\theta = 60°$, the signal repeats every 6 samples and its envelope falls to $1/e$ after $1/\ln(1/0.9) \approx 9.5$ samples.
Two poles at the same place give a factor $n$ in front of the exponential:

blocks.tex: n\, r^n u[n] \;\leftrightarrow\; \frac{r z^{-1}}{\left(1 - r z^{-1}\right)^2} = \frac{r z}{(z - r)^2}, \qquad |z| > r

blocks.text: The signal first rises (the $n$ wins) and then decays (the $r^n$ wins), peaking near $n = 1/\ln(1/r)$. A double pole on the unit circle, $n\, u[n]$, is a ramp that grows forever even though $1^n$ does not: repeated poles on the circle are unstable. In the viewer, pick ramped exponential n·rⁿu[n]; the z-plane panel marks the pole ×2.

A causal system is BIBO stable exactly when every pole of its transfer function lies strictly inside the unit circle. The geometric reason is the one on the Region of Convergence (#/math/z-transform/region-of-convergence) page: causal means the ROC is outside the outermost pole, stable means the unit circle is in the ROC, and both hold only if the outermost pole is inside the circle. A pole on the circle gives a signal that never dies out; a pole outside gives one that grows.

Continuous-time systems have the same story with a different shape. Sampling with period $T$ maps the s-plane to the z-plane by $z = e^{sT}$: the left half of the s-plane (stable continuous poles) lands inside the unit circle, the imaginary axis wraps round the unit circle, and a horizontal strip of height $2\pi/T$ covers the whole z-plane once. That wrapping is aliasing, seen geometrically.

blocks.title: Read a pole plot
blocks.text: A causal signal has poles at $0.8 e^{\pm j 90°}$ and nothing else. Describe the signal.
solution: Angle $90°$: it repeats every 4 samples. Radius 0.8: the envelope shrinks by 0.8 each sample, falling to $1/e$ after about $1/\ln(1.25) \approx 4.5$ samples. It is a damped oscillation with period 4, and it is stable.

blocks.title: Unstable or not?
blocks.text: Which of these causal transfer functions is stable? (a) $1/(1 - 1.1 z^{-1})$; (b) $1/(1 + 0.5z^{-1})$; (c) $1/(1 - z^{-1})^2$.
solution: (a) pole at 1.1, outside: unstable. (b) pole at $-0.5$, inside: stable, an alternating decay. (c) double pole at 1, on the circle: unstable, the ramp $(n+1)u[n]$.
